newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan seeks to limit fallout from Hashimoto remark.
newsitem.headline: Japan seeks to limit fallout from Hashimoto remark.

text.p: Japan sought on Tuesday to limit potential damage after a remark by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto sent U.S. financial markets reeling, but analysts said the provocative comment could haunt bilateral ties.

Hashimoto, responding to a question after a speech at Columbia University in New York on Monday, said Japan had in the past been tempted to sell its holdings of U.S. Treasury securities and boost its gold reserves, but had not done so.

"I hope the U.S. will engage in efforts and in cooperation to maintain exchange stability so we will not succumb to the temptation to sell off Treasury bills and switch our funds to gold," Hashimoto added.

The remark undermined the dollar in New York and ignited a sell-off in U.S. shares which sliced 192.25 points off the Dow Jones industrial average, a point decline second only to the 508-point drop when the market crashed on October 19, 1987.

In a statement dated June 23 and released on Tuesday in Tokyo, the Finance Ministry said Hashimoto had been misunderstood, that the prime minister regretted that his intentions had not been accurately conveyed. It said Japanese authorities would keep cooperating with the United States to maintain stable currency markets.

The remark by Hashimoto -- an outspoken politician who made a name with his tough stance as trade minister in bitter U.S.-Japan talks in 1995 -- appeared to reflect frustration at American criticism of Tokyo's tight fiscal stance and Washington's loud warnings to Japan not to let its trade surplus balloon again.

"America is putting very strong pressure on Japan. At the political level Japan's stance is to put up with this, but in economic circles and in society, people are getting...fed up," said political commentator Minoru Morita.

Hashimoto may also have been irked at Washington's failure to give high marks to his deregulation efforts, including his centre-piece "Big Bang" reforms aimed at boosting competition in Japan's stodgy financial markets, analysts added.

Speaking after the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations' summit in Denver, Colorado, on Sunday, U.S. President Bill Clinton warned Japan it risked economic war if its trade surplus ballooned again and took direct aim at the fiscal tightening which Hashimoto has pledged to carry out.

Faced with U.S. criticism, Hashimoto's quick temper may have prompted his provocative remark. "When he feels that he has been challenged...he tends to fight back," said Takeshi Kiuchi, chief economist at LTCB Research Institute.

But Japan is unlikely to follow through on Hashimoto's veiled threat -- which he has reportedly made before -- not least because the probable impact would be to boost the yen against the dollar and hurt Japan's exports and its economy.

"We would certainly see the dollar/yen much, much lower. We're talking new historic lows (for the dollar) if they started doing that," said Kenneth Landon, currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "I don't think that it reflects the intention of Japan to sell U.S. securities. It was mostly a sign of frustration with U.S. haggling over the trade issue."

Asian currency markets mostly shrugged off the comment and U.S. Treasuries recovered in Tokyo from their overnight fall on bargain-hunting, although the New York stock market drop kept Tokyo share prices weak in afternoon trade.
The comment could, however, harm U.S.-Japan ties by undermining mutual confidence. "I think Hashimoto misspoke and that it was not intentional," Morita said.

"The U.S. side has misgivings that Japan might sell its U.S. Treasuries and that concern will be strengthened. The U.S. will feel it cannot regard Japan as a completely faithful partner. This happening will have a considerably strong impact politically and economically," Morita added.

Hashimoto's remark -- perhaps intended to remind Washington that two-way ties are built on more than just trade numbers -- could backfire by giving U.S. proponents of a tough trade stance towards Tokyo the leverage needed to back up their views.
"I think he made an enormous diplomatic blunder," said Ron Bevacqua, senior economist at Merrill Lynch Japan.

"The U.S. administration has been talking big guns, but by and large they have been willing to accept the Japanese surplus because the U.S. unemployment rate is so low... Now it will be much harder to accept the Japanese trade surplus."
